newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France opens door to private retirement pensions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France opens door to private retirement pensions.

text.p: French legislators approved a bill on Friday to allow private pension funds in France, prising open an age-old regime of state-backed retirement to a multi-billion dollar business promising the stock market a new lease of life.

After years of heated controversy in a country that has long shunned an "Anglo-Saxon model" of huge, powerful private pension funds, the National Assembly backed a bill introducing a similar system, but 'a la francaise'.

"This will inject fresh dynamism into the French economy and thus into employment by redirecting French people's capital and savings," said Jean-Pierre Thomas, one of the main sponsors of the bill in parliament.
"This also provides an answer to a globalising economy and the advance of American pension funds which would 'colonise' our companies if we are not careful," he told reporters.

The bill, which must pass through the Senate before becoming law, went through the lower house of parliament with the backing of the RPR and UDF coalition partners. The opposition Socialist Party and Communists voted against.

The government insists that the legislation, which permits funds set up by agreement between employers and employees, will run in tandem and not replace the current system of universal pensions organised by the state.
The new private funds could start as early as next year and will be run by banks, insurance companies and mutual groups.

The legislation caps at 65 percent the amount of funds they are allowed to invest in government debt, circumventing European Union rules prohibiting quotas on equity investment and ensuring that large sums will be ploughed into the stock market.
For those who turn to the new system, the bill will allow them to write-off contributions against income tax to the tune of five percent of their gross salary.

It also allows for them to withdraw 20 percent of the money in a lump sum and the rest in annuities -- in a compromise which followed a fierce debate pitting banks, in favour of lump-sum payouts, against insurers who wanted payouts in annuities.

Unlike Britain and the United States, where pension funds are huge stock market players, France has so far depended very largely on a system where pensioners are paid by the state from the wages of those in work today.

The change comes at a time when governments across Europe are bent on cutting public deficits and increasingly questioning the ability of welfare systems to cope with the growing proportion of pensioners that comes with increased longevity.
The opposition Socialist party earlier this week slammed the French pension funds bill as "a new step in the attack against the welfare system."
The government says the pension funds will channel badly needed money into France's undercapitalised firms and a stock exchange which is tiny compared to those of London and New York.

"This is very good news for the Paris bourse," a spokesman for the French stock exchanges association said on Friday. "There will be a natural flow of investment into shares, which offer higher long-term returns."
French shares would attract a part, still hard to measure, of possibly 30 to 40 billion francs ($6-8 billion) in total investment flows, he said.
